notes.front: What is a hazard class?
notes.explanation: The class comes from the definitions in part 173 and from the § 172.101 table.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 171 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 171.8, “Hazard class”, p. 27
notes.evidence: Hazard class means the category of hazard assigned to a hazardous material under the definitional criteria of part 173 of this subchapter and the provisions of the § 172.101 table.
notes.back: The category of hazard assigned to a hazardous material under the part 173 criteria and the § 172.101 table.
notes.example: Like a sorting bin with nine slots: a material may fit the description of several slots, but it goes into one.

notes.front: What is an explosive (Class 1)?
notes.explanation: The definition covers things that were never meant to explode but can react that way, unless they are classed elsewhere in the regulations.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.50(a), p. 68
notes.evidence: an explosive means any substance or article, including a device, which is designed to function by explosion (i.e., an extremely rapid release of gas and heat) or which, by chemical reaction within itself, is able to function in a similar manner even if not designed to function by explosion
notes.back: A substance or article designed to function by explosion, or able to function in a similar way by chemical reaction within itself.
notes.example: Like a firework, which the definition names: the term includes pyrotechnic substances and articles unless they are otherwise classed.

notes.front: What is a mass explosion?
notes.explanation: Division 1.1 is defined by this hazard.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.50(b)(1), p. 68
notes.evidence: Division 1.1 consists of explosives that have a mass explosion hazard. A mass explosion is one which affects almost the entire load instantaneously.
notes.back: An explosion that affects almost the entire load instantaneously.
notes.example: Like a row of dominoes that all fall at the same instant, rather than one by one.

notes.front: What kind of explosive is placed in Division 1.1?
notes.explanation: Division 1.1 is defined by the mass explosion: almost the entire load goes off at once.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.50(b)(1), p. 68
notes.evidence: Division 1.1 consists of explosives that have a mass explosion hazard.
notes.back: An explosive that has a mass explosion hazard.
notes.example: Like a stack of crates that would all go up together if one did, not one crate at a time.

notes.front: What kind of explosive is placed in Division 1.2?
notes.explanation: The danger here is things being thrown out, not the whole load going off at once.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.50(b)(2), p. 68
notes.evidence: Division 1.2 consists of explosives that have a projection hazard but not a mass explosion hazard.
notes.back: An explosive with a projection hazard but not a mass explosion hazard.
notes.example: Like a crate that sends pieces flying if it goes off, while the crates beside it stay intact.

notes.front: What kind of explosive is placed in Division 1.3?
notes.explanation: Fire is the main danger in this division; blast and projection are only minor.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.50(b)(3), p. 68
notes.evidence: Division 1.3 consists of explosives that have a fire hazard and either a minor blast hazard or a minor projection hazard or both, but not a mass explosion hazard.
notes.back: An explosive with a fire hazard and a minor blast or minor projection hazard (or both), but no mass explosion hazard.
notes.example: Like a load that mostly burns fiercely, with only small bangs or small fragments.

notes.front: What kind of explosive is placed in Division 1.4?
notes.explanation: Its effects are largely confined to the package, and no fragments of appreciable size or range are expected.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.50(b)(4), p. 68
notes.evidence: Division 1.4 consists of explosives that present a minor explosion hazard. The explosive effects are largely confined to the package and no projection of fragments of appreciable size or range is to be expected.
notes.back: An explosive that presents a minor explosion hazard.
notes.example: Like a sealed box in which anything that goes off stays mostly inside the box.

notes.front: What kind of explosive is placed in Division 1.5?
notes.explanation: They could mass explode, but they are so insensitive that setting them off is very unlikely.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.50(b)(5), p. 68
notes.evidence: consists of very insensitive explosives. This division is comprised of substances which have a mass explosion hazard but are so insensitive that there is very little probability of initiation
notes.back: Very insensitive explosives: substances with a mass explosion hazard but very little probability of initiation.
notes.example: Like a Division 1.1 load that is very hard to set off.

notes.front: What kind of explosive is placed in Division 1.6?
notes.explanation: They mainly contain extremely insensitive substances and show a negligible probability of accidental initiation or propagation.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.50(b)(6), p. 69
notes.evidence: consists of extremely insensitive articles that do not have a mass explosion hazard. This division is comprised of articles which predominately contain extremely insensitive substances
notes.back: Extremely insensitive articles that do not have a mass explosion hazard.
notes.example: Like Division 1.5, but for articles rather than substances, and without the mass explosion hazard.

notes.front: What is a flammable gas (Division 2.1)?
notes.explanation: Two tests are set out: how little of it in air will ignite, and how wide its flammable range is.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.115(a), p. 104
notes.evidence: a flammable gas (Division 2.1) means any material which is a gas at 20 °C (68 °F) or less and 101.3 kPa (14.7 psia) of pressure
notes.back: Gas at 20 °C and 101.3 kPa that ignites at 13% or less in air, or whose flammable range is at least 12%.
notes.example: Like a gas that will light when only a small share of the air around it is that gas.

notes.front: What is a non-flammable, nonpoisonous compressed gas (Division 2.2)?
notes.explanation: Division 2.2 is defined by pressure and physical state, then by ruling out the flammable and poisonous gas divisions.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.115(b), p. 104
notes.evidence: Exerts in the packaging a gauge pressure of 200 kPa (29.0 psig/43.8 psia) or greater at 20 °C (68 °F), is a liquefied gas or is a cryogenic liquid
notes.back: A material at 200 kPa gauge or more at 20 °C, or a liquefied gas or cryogenic liquid, that is not Division 2.1 or 2.3.
notes.example: Like a cylinder whose gas will not burn and is not poisonous, but is still under real pressure.

notes.front: What does LC50 for acute toxicity on inhalation measure?
notes.explanation: It is a laboratory measure of how poisonous a material is to breathe, used to set the inhalation criteria.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.132(b)(3), p. 115
notes.evidence: LC50 for acute toxicity on inhalation means that concentration of vapor, mist, or dust which, administered by continuous inhalation for one hour to both male and female young adult albino rats, causes death within 14 days in half of the animals tested.
uses: LC50 for acute toxicity on inhalation
notes.back: The concentration of vapour, mist or dust that, inhaled for one hour, kills half the young adult albino rats tested within 14 days.
notes.example: Like a dose rating for air: the lower the LC50, the less of the material in air it takes to be lethal.
introduces: LC50 for acute toxicity on inhalation

notes.front: What is a gas poisonous by inhalation (Division 2.3)?
notes.explanation: The presumption applies when human data are lacking and the gas has an LC50 of not more than 5000 mL/m3 in laboratory animals.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.115(c), p. 105
notes.evidence: Is known to be so toxic to humans as to pose a hazard to health during transportation, or (2) In the absence of adequate data on human toxicity, is presumed to be toxic to humans
uses: LC50 for acute toxicity on inhalation
notes.back: A gas known to be so toxic to humans that it is a health hazard in transport, or presumed toxic from animal tests.
notes.example: Like Division 2.1, it is defined for gases, but by toxicity rather than by flammability.

notes.front: What is a flash point?
notes.explanation: Class 3 and combustible liquids are both defined by flash point, so it is the figure that sorts liquids.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.120(c)(1), p. 107
notes.evidence: Flash point means the minimum temperature at which a liquid gives off vapor within a test vessel in sufficient concentration to form an ignitable mixture with air near the surface of the liquid.
notes.back: The minimum temperature at which a liquid gives off enough vapour in a test vessel to form an ignitable mixture with air near its surface.
notes.example: Like a threshold on a thermometer: below it the vapour above the liquid will not ignite; at it, it can.

notes.front: What is a flammable liquid (Class 3)?
notes.explanation: The definition also takes in some liquids heated in bulk to or above their flash point.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.120(a), p. 106
notes.evidence: a flammable liquid (Class 3) means a liquid having a flash point of not more than 60 °C (140 °F)
notes.back: A liquid with a flash point of not more than 60 °C (140 °F), subject to listed exceptions.
notes.example: Like a liquid tested at a flash point of 30 °C: well under the 60 °C line, so Class 3 unless an exception applies.

notes.front: What is a combustible liquid?
notes.explanation: Its flash point band starts where the Class 3 limit of 60 °C ends.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.120(b)(1), p. 106
notes.evidence: a combustible liquid means any liquid that does not meet the definition of any other hazard class specified in this subchapter and has a flash point above 60 °C (140 °F) and below 93 °C (200 °F).
notes.back: A liquid that meets no other hazard class and has a flash point above 60 °C (140 °F) and below 93 °C (200 °F).
notes.example: Like a liquid tested at a flash point of 80 °C that is not corrosive, toxic or anything else.

notes.front: What is a flammable solid (Division 4.1)?
notes.explanation: Division 4.1 is defined as a list of types, not by one test.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.124(a), p. 109
notes.evidence: flammable solid (Division 4.1) means any of the following four types of materials
notes.back: Any of four types: desensitized explosives, self-reactive materials, readily combustible solids and polymerizing materials.
notes.example: Like a folder with four tabs: each tab has its own criteria.

notes.front: What is a pyrophoric material?
notes.explanation: It is one of the two kinds of Division 4.2 material.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.124(b)(1), p. 111
notes.evidence: A pyrophoric material is a liquid or solid that, even in small quantities and without an external ignition source,
notes.back: A liquid or solid that, even in small quantities and with no outside ignition source, can ignite within five minutes of contact with air.
notes.example: Like a material that catches fire simply because its container was opened to the air.

notes.front: What is a spontaneously combustible material (Division 4.2)?
notes.explanation: Both kinds can ignite without an outside flame: one on contact with air, the other by heating itself up.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.124(b), p. 111
notes.evidence: Division 4.2 (Spontaneously Combustible Material). For the purposes of this subchapter, spontaneously combustible material (Division 4.2) means— (1) A pyrophoric material.
notes.back: A pyrophoric material or a self-heating material.
notes.example: Like a heap of material that slowly warms itself through reaction with air until it catches fire.

notes.front: What is a dangerous when wet material (Division 4.3)?
notes.explanation: The hazard comes from reaction with water, so the test measures gas given off per kilogram per hour.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.124(c), p. 111
notes.evidence: dangerous when wet material (Division 4.3) means a material that, by contact with water, is liable to become spontaneously flammable or to give off flammable or toxic gas
notes.back: A material that, in contact with water, is liable to become spontaneously flammable or to give off flammable or toxic gas above a set rate.
notes.example: Like a solid that fizzes out a flammable gas when rain gets into its drum.

notes.front: What is an oxidizer (Division 5.1)?
notes.explanation: The danger is to what is around it: it feeds the burning of other materials.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.127(a), p. 112
notes.evidence: oxidizer (Division 5.1) means a material that may, generally by yielding oxygen, cause or enhance the combustion of other materials.
notes.back: A material that may, generally by yielding oxygen, cause or enhance the combustion of other materials.
notes.example: Like bellows on a fire: it is not the fuel, but it makes the fuel burn harder.

notes.front: What is an organic peroxide (Division 5.2)?
notes.explanation: In the derivative, one or more hydrogen atoms of hydrogen peroxide have been replaced by organic radicals.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.128(a), p. 114
notes.evidence: -O-O- structure and which may be considered a derivative of hydrogen peroxide, where one or more of the hydrogen atoms have been replaced by organic radicals
notes.back: An organic compound with oxygen in the bivalent -O-O- structure, which may be seen as a derivative of hydrogen peroxide.
notes.example: Like hydrogen peroxide with an organic group swapped in for a hydrogen atom.

notes.front: What is the median lethal dose (LD50) for acute oral toxicity?
notes.explanation: It is expressed as mass of substance per mass of test animal (mg/kg), so a lower figure means a more toxic material.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.132(b)(1), p. 115
notes.evidence: LD50 (median lethal dose) for acute oral toxicity is the statistically derived single dose of a substance that can be expected to cause death within 14 days in 50% of young adult albino rats when administered by the oral route.
uses: LC50 for acute toxicity on inhalation
notes.back: The single dose, given by mouth, expected to kill 50% of young adult albino rats within 14 days.
notes.example: Like LC50, but for a dose swallowed rather than a concentration breathed.

notes.front: What is a poisonous material (Division 6.1)?
notes.explanation: Toxic gases are defined separately, as Division 2.3.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.132(a), p. 115
notes.evidence: poisonous material (Division 6.1) means a material, other than a gas, which is known to be so toxic to humans as to afford a hazard to health during transportation
notes.back: A material other than a gas, known to be so toxic to humans that it is a health hazard in transport, or presumed so.
notes.example: Like Division 2.3, but for liquids and solids.

notes.front: What is an infectious substance (Division 6.2)?
notes.explanation: A pathogen is a microorganism, such as a bacterium, virus, parasite or fungus, or another agent such as a prion, that can cause disease in humans or animals.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.134(a)(1), p. 120
notes.evidence: Division 6.2 (Infectious substance) means a material known or reasonably expected to contain a pathogen.
notes.back: A material known or reasonably expected to contain a pathogen.
notes.example: Like a sample that may carry a virus able to make people or animals ill.

notes.front: What is a Category A infectious substance?
notes.explanation: Category A is the higher of the two Division 6.2 categories, defined by what exposure could do to healthy people or animals.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.134(a)(1)(i), p. 120
notes.evidence: Category A: An infectious substance in a form capable of causing permanent disability or life-threatening or fatal disease in otherwise healthy humans or animals when exposure to it occurs.
notes.back: One in a form capable of causing permanent disability or life-threatening or fatal disease in otherwise healthy humans or animals when exposure occurs.
notes.example: Like the top shelf of a laboratory freezer, kept for what could cause lasting harm or death after one exposure.

notes.front: What is a Category B infectious substance?
notes.explanation: It is defined as whatever infectious substance does not reach the Category A level.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.134(a)(1)(ii), p. 121
notes.evidence: Category B: An infectious substance that is not in a form generally capable of causing permanent disability or life-threatening or fatal disease in otherwise healthy humans or animals when exposure to it occurs.
notes.back: An infectious substance that is not in a form generally capable of causing permanent disability or life-threatening or fatal disease when exposure occurs.
notes.example: Like the other shelf: infectious, but not generally able to cause lasting or fatal harm on exposure.

notes.front: What is a radioactive material (Class 7)?
notes.explanation: Both tests must be exceeded; a material that passes only one is not radioactive material for these rules.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.403, p. 307
notes.evidence: Radioactive material means any material containing radionuclides where both the activity concentration and the total activity in the consignment exceed the values specified in the table in § 173.436
notes.back: Material containing radionuclides where both activity concentration and total activity in the consignment exceed the § 173.436 values.
notes.example: Like a two-key lock: the concentration and the total amount both have to be over the line.

notes.front: What is a corrosive material (Class 8)?
notes.explanation: The skin test is the main route in; a liquid, or a solid that may become liquid in transport, is also corrosive if it has a severe corrosion rate on steel or aluminium.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.136(a), p. 124
notes.evidence: ‘‘corrosive material’’ (Class 8) means a liquid or solid that causes irreversible damage to human skin at the site of contact within a specified period of time.
notes.back: A liquid or solid that causes irreversible damage to human skin at the site of contact within a specified time.
notes.example: Like an acid that leaves a lasting burn where it touches the skin.

notes.front: What is a miscellaneous hazardous material (Class 9)?
notes.explanation: Class 9 catches hazards that none of Classes 1 to 8 describe.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.140, p. 127
notes.evidence: miscellaneous hazardous material (Class 9) means a material which presents a hazard during transportation but which does not meet the definition of any other hazard class.
notes.back: A material that presents a hazard during transportation but does not meet the definition of any other hazard class.
notes.example: Like the “other” box on a form: used only when no other box fits.

notes.front: A material may meet the defining criteria for more than one hazard class, but it is assigned to {{c1::only one}} hazard class.
notes.explanation: The other hazards are not lost: the classification rules decide which one becomes the class.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 171 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 171.8, “Hazard class”, p. 27
notes.evidence: A material may meet the defining criteria for more than one hazard class but is assigned to only one hazard class.

notes.front: In what two ways may the hazard class of a hazardous material be shown?
notes.explanation: Section 173.2 lists each class and division with its number, its name and the section that defines it.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.2, p. 5
notes.evidence: The hazard class of a hazardous material is indicated by either the class or division number or the class name.
notes.back: By the class or division number, or by the class name.

notes.front: How many divisions does Class 1 (explosives) have?
notes.explanation: Each division describes a different way an explosive can behave, from mass explosion to extremely insensitive articles.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.50(b), p. 68
notes.evidence: Explosives in Class 1 are divided into six divisions as follows:
notes.back: Six: Divisions 1.1 to 1.6.

notes.front: Which three divisions make up Class 2 (gases)?
notes.explanation: Section 173.115 defines all three divisions of Class 2 together.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.115, p. 104
notes.evidence: § 173.115 Class 2, Divisions 2.1, 2.2, and 2.3—Definitions. (a) Division 2.1 (Flammable gas).
notes.back: 2.1 flammable gas; 2.2 non-flammable, nonpoisonous compressed gas; 2.3 gas poisonous by inhalation.

notes.front: Which three divisions make up Class 4?
notes.explanation: Section 173.124 defines all three Class 4 divisions together.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.124, p. 109
notes.evidence: § 173.124 Class 4, Divisions 4.1, 4.2 and 4.3—Definitions. (a) Division 4.1 (Flammable Solid).
notes.back: 4.1 flammable solid; 4.2 spontaneously combustible material; 4.3 dangerous when wet material.

notes.front: Which two divisions make up Class 5?
notes.explanation: Each Class 5 division has its own section: § 173.127 for oxidizers and § 173.128 for organic peroxides.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.127, p. 112
notes.evidence: § 173.127 Class 5, Division 5.1—Definition and assignment of packing groups. (a) Definition. For the purpose of this subchapter, oxidizer (Division 5.1)
notes.back: Division 5.1, oxidizer, and Division 5.2, organic peroxide.

notes.front: Which two divisions make up Class 6?
notes.explanation: Section 173.132 defines Division 6.1; Division 6.2 is defined in § 173.134.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.132, p. 115
notes.evidence: § 173.132 Class 6, Division 6.1—Definitions. (a) For the purpose of this subchapter, poisonous material (Division 6.1) means a material, other than a gas
notes.back: Division 6.1, poisonous material, and Division 6.2, infectious substance.

notes.front: For Class 1, “explosion” means an extremely rapid release of {{c1::gas and heat}}.
notes.explanation: The definition spells this out in brackets after the word “explosion”.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.50(a), p. 68
notes.evidence: which is designed to function by explosion (i.e., an extremely rapid release of gas and heat)

notes.front: Does the term “explosive” include pyrotechnic substances and articles?
notes.explanation: Pyrotechnics are named in the definition itself, with the same “otherwise classed” exception as other explosives.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.50(a), p. 68
notes.evidence: The term includes a pyrotechnic substance or article, unless the substance or article is otherwise classed under the provisions of this subchapter.
notes.back: Yes, unless the substance or article is otherwise classed under the regulations.

notes.front: What must happen before anyone may offer or transport an explosive, unless the subpart says otherwise?
notes.explanation: Section 173.51 makes testing and approval the gate for putting an explosive into transport.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.51(a), p. 69
notes.evidence: no person may offer for transportation or transport an explosive, unless it has been tested and classed and approved by the Associate Administrator (§ 173.56).
notes.back: It must be tested, classed and approved by the Associate Administrator.

notes.front: A company has developed a new explosive article. It has not yet been tested or approved, and no exception in the subpart covers it. May it be offered for transportation?
notes.explanation: Section 173.51 bars offering or transporting an explosive until it has been tested, classed and approved.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.51(a), p. 69
notes.evidence: no person may offer for transportation or transport an explosive, unless it has been tested and classed and approved by the Associate Administrator (§ 173.56).
notes.back: C: No: it must first be tested, classed and approved by the Associate Administrator
notes.choices:
A) Yes, if it is packed as Division 1.4
B) Yes, if it travels by highway only
C) No: it must first be tested, classed and approved by the Associate Administrator
D) Yes, if the maker certifies it is safe
notes.choicesExplained: A: the shipper cannot choose a division before the explosive has been tested, classed and approved. B: the approval rule is not limited to any one mode. D: the approval must come from the Associate Administrator, not from the maker.

notes.front: What makes up the classification code of an explosive?
notes.explanation: The compatibility group letter controls which explosives may be carried or stored together.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.52(a), p. 69
notes.evidence: The classification code for an explosive, which is assigned by the Associate Administrator in accordance with this subpart, consists of the division number followed by the compatibility group letter.
notes.back: The division number followed by the compatibility group letter.

notes.front: For a Division 1.4 package, what must an external fire not cause?
notes.explanation: The test is about a fire outside the package, not inside it.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.50(b)(4), p. 68
notes.evidence: An external fire must not cause virtually instantaneous explosion of almost the entire contents of the package.
notes.back: Virtually instantaneous explosion of almost the entire contents of the package.

notes.front: Division 1.6 articles show a {{c1::negligible}} probability of accidental initiation or propagation.
notes.explanation: That is what makes them extremely insensitive articles.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.50(b)(6), p. 69
notes.evidence: articles which predominately contain extremely insensitive substances and that demonstrate a negligible probability of accidental initiation or propagation.

notes.front: Tests on an explosive article show that if one article functions, fragments are thrown some distance, but the rest of the load does not go off with it. Which division fits?
notes.explanation: A projection hazard without a mass explosion hazard is the Division 1.2 definition.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.50(b)(2), p. 68
notes.evidence: Division 1.2 consists of explosives that have a projection hazard but not a mass explosion hazard.
notes.back: B: Division 1.2
notes.choices:
A) Division 1.1
B) Division 1.2
C) Division 1.4
D) Division 1.5
notes.choicesExplained: A: needs a mass explosion hazard, where almost the entire load goes off instantaneously. C: is for effects largely confined to the package, with no fragments of appreciable size or range. D: is for very insensitive substances that do have a mass explosion hazard.

notes.front: Testing shows that if a substance in a vehicle load initiates, almost the whole load explodes at once. It is not especially insensitive. Which division fits?
notes.explanation: Almost the entire load going off instantaneously is a mass explosion, which defines Division 1.1.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.50(b)(1), p. 68
notes.evidence: Division 1.1 consists of explosives that have a mass explosion hazard. A mass explosion is one which affects almost the entire load instantaneously.
notes.back: C: Division 1.1
notes.choices:
A) Division 1.5
B) Division 1.3
C) Division 1.1
D) Division 1.6
notes.choicesExplained: B: has only a minor blast or projection hazard and no mass explosion hazard. A: would need the substance to be so insensitive that initiation is very unlikely. D: is for extremely insensitive articles with no mass explosion hazard.

notes.front: An explosive mainly burns fiercely when it functions, with only a minor blast. It has no mass explosion hazard. Which division fits?
notes.explanation: A fire hazard with a minor blast or projection hazard, and no mass explosion hazard, is Division 1.3.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.50(b)(3), p. 68
notes.evidence: Division 1.3 consists of explosives that have a fire hazard and either a minor blast hazard or a minor projection hazard or both, but not a mass explosion hazard.
notes.back: B: Division 1.3
notes.choices:
A) Division 1.1
B) Division 1.3
C) Division 1.6
D) Division 1.2
notes.choicesExplained: A: is for explosives with a mass explosion hazard. D: is for a projection hazard, not a fire hazard with a minor blast. C: is for extremely insensitive articles, not for a fire hazard.

notes.front: When a packaged explosive article functions, the effect stays largely inside its package and no sizeable fragments fly out. Which division fits?
notes.explanation: A minor explosion hazard with effects largely confined to the package is the Division 1.4 definition.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.50(b)(4), p. 68
notes.evidence: Division 1.4 consists of explosives that present a minor explosion hazard. The explosive effects are largely confined to the package
notes.back: B: Division 1.4
notes.choices:
A) Division 1.2
B) Division 1.4
C) Division 1.3
D) Division 1.5
notes.choicesExplained: A: is for a projection hazard, where fragments are thrown. C: is for a fire hazard with a minor blast or projection hazard. D: is for very insensitive substances with a mass explosion hazard.

notes.front: A blasting substance would mass explode if it ever detonated, but it is so insensitive that there is very little probability of initiation in normal transport. Which division fits?
notes.explanation: A mass explosion hazard in a substance so insensitive that initiation is very unlikely is the Division 1.5 definition.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.50(b)(5), p. 68

notes.back: C: Division 1.5

A) Division 1.1
B) Division 1.4
C) Division 1.5
D) Division 1.6

notes.front: Division 1.5 and Division 1.6 are both very or extremely insensitive. What two differences separate them?
notes.explanation: The definitions differ both in what is carried (substances or articles) and in whether a mass explosion hazard exists.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.50(b)(5)–(6), p. 68
notes.evidence: This division is comprised of substances which have a mass explosion hazard but are so insensitive that there is very little probability of initiation
notes.back: 1.5 is substances with a mass explosion hazard; 1.6 is articles without a mass explosion hazard.

notes.front: A gas is Division 2.1 if it is ignitable at 101.3 kPa when in a mixture of {{c1::13 percent or less}} by volume with air.
notes.explanation: This is the first of two alternative tests; meeting either one is enough.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.115(a)(1), p. 104
notes.evidence: Is ignitable at 101.3 kPa (14.7 psia) when in a mixture of 13 percent or less by volume with air; or

notes.front: A gas is also Division 2.1 if its flammable range with air at 101.3 kPa is at least {{c1::12 percent}}, whatever the lower limit.
notes.explanation: This second test catches gases whose lower limit is above 13 percent but whose flammable range is wide.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.115(a)(2), p. 104
notes.evidence: Has a flammable range at 101.3 kPa (14.7 psia) with air of at least 12 percent regardless of the lower limit.

notes.front: Division 2.2 covers a gas that exerts a gauge pressure of {{c1::200 kPa}} (29.0 psig) or greater at 20 °C in the packaging, or is a liquefied gas or cryogenic liquid.
notes.explanation: The figure is a gauge pressure at 20 °C; the regulation also gives it as 43.8 psia.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.115(b)(1), p. 104
notes.evidence: Exerts in the packaging a gauge pressure of 200 kPa (29.0 psig/43.8 psia) or greater at 20 °C (68 °F), is a liquefied gas or is a cryogenic liquid, and

notes.front: What are two kinds of gas that the Division 2.2 heading expressly includes?
notes.explanation: The heading lists all of these, so an oxidizing gas that is neither flammable nor poisonous can still be Division 2.2.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.115(b), p. 104
notes.evidence: Division 2.2 (non-flammable, nonpoisonous compressed gas—including compressed gas, liquefied gas, pressurized cryogenic gas, compressed gas in solution, asphyxiant gas and oxidizing gas).
notes.back: Any two of: compressed, liquefied, pressurized cryogenic, in solution, asphyxiant, oxidizing gas.

notes.front: Without adequate human data, a gas is presumed toxic (Division 2.3) if laboratory animals show an LC50 of not more than {{c1::5000 mL/m3}}.
notes.explanation: The presumption is used only when adequate data on human toxicity are missing.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.115(c)(2), p. 105
notes.evidence: is presumed to be toxic to humans because when tested on laboratory animals it has an LC50 value of not more than 5000 mL/m3
uses: LC50 for acute toxicity on inhalation

notes.front: A gas at 20 °C ignites in air when it makes up 9 percent of the mixture by volume. It is not known to be toxic and its LC50 is far above 5000 mL/m3. Which division fits?
notes.explanation: Ignitable at 13 percent or less by volume in air meets the first Division 2.1 test.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.115(a)(1), p. 104
notes.evidence: Is ignitable at 101.3 kPa (14.7 psia) when in a mixture of 13 percent or less by volume with air; or
uses: LC50 for acute toxicity on inhalation
notes.back: C: Division 2.1
notes.choices:
A) Division 2.2
B) Division 2.3
C) Division 2.1
D) Class 3
notes.choicesExplained: A: is only for gases that meet neither the Division 2.1 nor the Division 2.3 definition. B: needs toxicity: known human toxicity or an LC50 of not more than 5000 mL/m3. D: is for liquids, not for a material that is a gas at 20 °C.

notes.front: Cylinders hold a gas at 15,000 kPa gauge at 20 °C. The gas does not burn and is not toxic. Which division fits?
notes.explanation: Pressure of at least 200 kPa gauge at 20 °C, with no Division 2.1 or 2.3 hazard, is Division 2.2.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.115(b), p. 104
notes.evidence: Exerts in the packaging a gauge pressure of 200 kPa (29.0 psig/43.8 psia) or greater at 20 °C (68 °F), is a liquefied gas or is a cryogenic liquid
uses: LC50 for acute toxicity on inhalation
notes.back: A: Division 2.2
notes.choices:
A) Division 2.2
B) Division 2.1
C) Division 2.3
D) It is not regulated because it is not flammable or toxic
notes.choicesExplained: B: needs the gas to be ignitable at 13 percent or less, or to have a 12 percent flammable range. C: needs known human toxicity or an LC50 of not more than 5000 mL/m3. D: a gauge pressure of 200 kPa or more at 20 °C is enough to meet the Division 2.2 definition.

notes.front: No human data exist for a new gas. Tests on laboratory animals give an LC50 of 2,500 mL/m3. It does not burn. Which division fits?
notes.explanation: An LC50 of not more than 5000 mL/m3 makes the gas presumed toxic to humans.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.115(c)(2), p. 105
notes.evidence: In the absence of adequate data on human toxicity, is presumed to be toxic to humans because when tested on laboratory animals it has an LC50 value of not more than 5000 mL/m3
uses: LC50 for acute toxicity on inhalation
notes.back: C: Division 2.3
notes.choices:
A) Division 2.1
B) Division 2.2
C) Division 2.3
D) Division 6.1
notes.choicesExplained: A: needs a flammability result, and this gas does not burn. B: applies only to gases that do not meet the Division 2.3 definition. D: is for materials other than gases.

notes.front: Besides liquids with a flash point of not more than 60 °C, what else meets the Class 3 definition?
notes.explanation: Heating such a liquid past its flash point brings it into Class 3 even though its flash point is higher.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.120(a), p. 106
notes.evidence: any material in a liquid phase with a flash point at or above 37.8 °C (100 °F) that is intentionally heated and offered for transportation or transported at or above its flash point in a bulk packaging
notes.back: A liquid with a flash point at or above 37.8 °C intentionally heated to or above its flash point in a bulk packaging.

notes.front: A liquid has a flash point above 35 °C and is in a water-miscible solution with more than 90 percent water by mass. Is it Class 3?
notes.explanation: Section 173.120(a) lists it with other exceptions, such as liquids above 35 °C that do not sustain combustion.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.120(a)(5), p. 106
notes.evidence: Any liquid with a flash point greater than 35 °C (95 °F) which is in a water-miscible solution with a water content of more than 90 percent by mass.
notes.back: No. It is one of the listed exceptions to the Class 3 definition.

notes.front: Which Class 3 liquids may be reclassed as combustible liquids?
notes.explanation: The reclass is an option (“may”), not an obligation.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.120(b)(2), p. 106
notes.evidence: A flammable liquid with a flash point at or above 38 °C (100 °F) that does not meet the definition of any other hazard class may be reclassed as a combustible liquid.
notes.back: A flammable liquid with a flash point at or above 38 °C (100 °F) that meets no other hazard class.

notes.front: For which modes is the reclass of a flammable liquid as a combustible liquid not allowed?
notes.explanation: The reclass option is written for the other modes, such as highway.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.120(b)(2), p. 106
notes.evidence: This provision does not apply to transportation by vessel or aircraft, except where other
notes.back: Vessel and aircraft, except where other means of transport are impracticable.

notes.front: A liquid with a flash point of 45 °C meets no other hazard class. It will go by highway only. How may it be classed?
notes.explanation: The flash point is within the Class 3 limit, and the 38 °C reclass option applies outside vessel and aircraft transport.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.120(b)(2), p. 106
notes.evidence: A flammable liquid with a flash point at or above 38 °C (100 °F) that does not meet the definition of any other hazard class may be reclassed as a combustible liquid.
notes.back: C: As Class 3, or it may be reclassed as a combustible liquid
notes.choices:
A) Only as Class 3; reclassing is never allowed
B) Only as a combustible liquid, because 45 °C is above 38 °C
C) As Class 3, or it may be reclassed as a combustible liquid
D) It is not regulated, because its flash point is above 35 °C
notes.choicesExplained: A: a flammable liquid with a flash point at or above 38 °C may be reclassed, except by vessel or aircraft. B: the reclass is optional; the liquid is Class 3 by definition. D: a flash point of not more than 60 °C meets the Class 3 definition unless a listed exception applies.

notes.front: A liquid meets no other hazard class and has a flash point of 75 °C. What is it?
notes.explanation: Its flash point falls in the band above 60 °C and below 93 °C.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.120(b)(1), p. 106
notes.evidence: has a flash point above 60 °C (140 °F) and below 93 °C (200 °F).
notes.back: A: A combustible liquid
notes.choices:
A) A combustible liquid
B) A Class 3 flammable liquid
C) A Class 9 miscellaneous hazardous material
D) Not a hazardous material at all
notes.choicesExplained: B: Class 3 stops at a flash point of 60 °C. C: combustible liquids have their own definition, which this liquid meets. D: a flash point above 60 °C and below 93 °C meets the combustible liquid definition.

notes.front: A liquid with a flash point of 50 °C meets no other hazard class. It will travel by vessel, and other means of transport are practicable. How is it classed?
notes.explanation: Its flash point is within the Class 3 limit, and the reclass option is shut off for vessel transport here.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.120(b)(2), p. 106
notes.evidence: This provision does not apply to transportation by vessel or aircraft, except where other
notes.back: B: As Class 3; it may not be reclassed as a combustible liquid
notes.choices:
A) As a combustible liquid, because its flash point is above 38 °C
B) As Class 3; it may not be reclassed as a combustible liquid
C) As a combustible liquid, because its flash point is above 35 °C
D) Not regulated, because vessel rules differ
notes.choicesExplained: A: the reclass does not apply to transport by vessel or aircraft when other means are practicable. C: 35 °C is not the combustible liquid line; combustible liquids start above 60 °C. D: the Class 3 definition has no mode limit; only the reclass option is limited.

notes.front: Flammable liquid or combustible liquid: where is the dividing line?
notes.explanation: Both are defined by flash point, and the combustible band starts where Class 3 ends.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.120(a)–(b), p. 106
notes.evidence: a flammable liquid (Class 3) means a liquid having a flash point of not more than 60 °C (140 °F)
notes.back: 60 °C (140 °F): not more than 60 °C is Class 3; above 60 °C and below 93 °C is a combustible liquid.

notes.front: A liquid meets no other hazard class. Its flash point is 95 °C. Which flash point definition does it meet?
notes.explanation: 95 °C is above both the Class 3 limit and the top of the combustible liquid band.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.120(b)(1), p. 106
notes.evidence: has a flash point above 60 °C (140 °F) and below 93 °C (200 °F).
notes.back: D: Neither Class 3 nor combustible liquid
notes.choices:
A) Class 3
B) Combustible liquid
C) Both, depending on the mode
D) Neither Class 3 nor combustible liquid
notes.choicesExplained: A: Class 3 stops at a flash point of 60 °C. B: the combustible band stops below 93 °C. C: the mode matters only for the reclass option, not for these limits.

notes.front: Which Division 4.1 type is made of explosives wetted with water, alcohol or plasticizer to suppress their explosive properties?
notes.explanation: Wetting suppresses the explosive properties of what would otherwise be explosives.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.124(a)(1), p. 109
notes.evidence: which are wetted with sufficient water, alcohol, or plasticizer to suppress explosive properties
notes.back: Desensitized explosives.

notes.front: Which Division 4.1 type is thermally unstable and can decompose exothermically even without oxygen (air)?
notes.explanation: Their decomposition gives off heat without needing air.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.124(a)(2)(i), p. 109
notes.evidence: Self-reactive materials that are thermally unstable and can undergo an exothermic decomposition even without participation of oxygen (air).
notes.back: Self-reactive materials.

notes.front: Which Division 4.1 type includes solids that may cause a fire through friction, such as matches?
notes.explanation: The type also covers fast-burning solids and certain metal powders, measured by burning tests.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.124(a)(3), p. 111
notes.evidence: Readily combustible solids are materials that— (i) Are solids which may cause a fire through friction, such as matches;
notes.back: Readily combustible solids.

notes.front: Which Division 4.1 type is liable, without stabilization, to an exothermic reaction that forms larger molecules or polymers in normal transport conditions?
notes.explanation: They count as Division 4.1 only when set temperature and heat-of-reaction criteria are met and they meet no Class 1 to 8 definition.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.124(a)(4), p. 111
notes.evidence: Polymerizing materials are materials which, without stabilization, are liable to undergo an exothermic reaction resulting in the formation of larger molecules or resulting in the formation of polymers under conditions normally encountered in transport.
notes.back: Polymerizing materials.

notes.front: A solid is a readily combustible solid if it shows a burning rate faster than {{c1::2.2 mm}} (0.087 inches) per second in the prescribed test.
notes.explanation: Metal powders use a different test: whether the reaction spreads along the whole sample in 10 minutes or less.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.124(a)(3)(ii), p. 111
notes.evidence: Show a burning rate faster than 2.2 mm (0.087 inches) per second when tested in accordance with the UN Manual of Tests and Criteria

notes.front: A pyrophoric material can ignite within {{c1::five minutes}} after coming into contact with air, even in small quantities and without an external ignition source.
notes.explanation: Pyrophoric materials are the first of the two kinds of Division 4.2 material.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.124(b)(1), p. 111
notes.evidence: can ignite within five (5) minutes after coming in contact with air when tested according to UN Manual of Tests and Criteria.

notes.front: How does a self-heating material become a fire risk?
notes.explanation: This is the second kind of Division 4.2 material, beside pyrophoric materials.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.124(b)(2), p. 111
notes.evidence: If the rate of heat production exceeds the rate of heat loss, then the temperature of the substance will rise which, after an induction time, may lead to self-ignition and combustion.
notes.back: Its slow reaction with oxygen in air makes heat; if heat is produced faster than lost, it warms and may self-ignite.

notes.front: A material is Division 4.3 if, in contact with water, it gives off flammable or toxic gas at a rate greater than {{c1::1 L per kilogram per hour}}, or is liable to become spontaneously flammable.
notes.explanation: The rate is measured under the United Nations Manual of Tests and Criteria.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.124(c), p. 111
notes.evidence: to give off flammable or toxic gas at a rate greater than 1 L per kilogram of the material, per hour, when tested in accordance with UN Manual of Tests and Criteria.

notes.front: A small amount of a powder, with no flame or spark nearby, bursts into flame about two minutes after its tin is opened to the air. Which division fits?
notes.explanation: Igniting within five minutes of contact with air without an ignition source makes it pyrophoric, which is Division 4.2.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.124(b)(1), p. 111
notes.evidence: A pyrophoric material is a liquid or solid that, even in small quantities and without an external ignition source,
notes.back: B: Division 4.2
notes.choices:
A) Division 4.1
B) Division 4.2
C) Division 4.3
D) Division 5.1
notes.choicesExplained: A: covers desensitized explosives, self-reactive, readily combustible and polymerizing materials, not ignition on contact with air. C: is about reaction with water, not with air. D: is about making other materials burn, generally by yielding oxygen.

notes.front: In testing, a solid in contact with water gives off a flammable gas at 5 L per kilogram per hour. It does not ignite in air. Which division fits?
notes.explanation: Giving off flammable gas with water at more than 1 L per kilogram per hour meets the Division 4.3 definition.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.124(c), p. 111
notes.evidence: to give off flammable or toxic gas at a rate greater than 1 L per kilogram of the material, per hour
notes.back: C: Division 4.3
notes.choices:
A) Division 4.1
B) Division 4.2
C) Division 4.3
D) Division 2.1
notes.choicesExplained: A: does not turn on reaction with water. B: is for materials that ignite in air or self-heat. D: is for materials that are themselves gases at 20 °C.

notes.front: A granular solid (not a metal powder) burns in the test at 3 mm per second. It does not react with water or air. Which division fits?
notes.explanation: A burning rate faster than 2.2 mm per second makes it a readily combustible solid, one of the four Division 4.1 types.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.124(a)(3)(ii), p. 111
notes.evidence: Show a burning rate faster than 2.2 mm (0.087 inches) per second
notes.back: B: Division 4.1
notes.choices:
A) Division 4.2
B) Division 4.1
C) Class 9
D) Division 4.3
notes.choicesExplained: A: is for pyrophoric or self-heating materials. D: is for materials that react with water. C: is only for materials that meet no other hazard class, and this one meets Division 4.1.

notes.front: An organic peroxide also meets the definition of an explosive. How must it be classed?
notes.explanation: Meeting the explosive definition is one of the listed cases that takes a material out of Division 5.2.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.128(a)(1), p. 114
notes.evidence: The material meets the definition of an explosive as prescribed in subpart C of this part, in which case it must be classed as an explosive;
notes.back: As an explosive.

notes.front: A granular material does not burn well on its own, but tests show that it makes cellulose burn faster by giving off oxygen. It is not an organic compound. Which division fits?
notes.explanation: Causing or enhancing the combustion of other materials, generally by yielding oxygen, is the oxidizer definition.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.127(a), p. 112
notes.evidence: oxidizer (Division 5.1) means a material that may, generally by yielding oxygen, cause or enhance the combustion of other materials.
notes.back: B: Division 5.1
notes.choices:
A) Division 5.2
B) Division 5.1
C) Division 4.1
D) Division 4.2
notes.choicesExplained: A: needs an organic compound with the -O-O- structure. C: is for materials that are themselves flammable solids of the four listed types. D: is for pyrophoric or self-heating materials.

notes.front: Oxidizer (5.1) or organic peroxide (5.2): what feature decides Division 5.2?
notes.explanation: Division 5.1 is defined by effect (feeding combustion); Division 5.2 is defined by chemical structure.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.128(a), p. 113
notes.evidence: organic peroxide (Division 5.2) means any organic compound containing oxygen (O) in the bivalent
notes.back: An organic compound containing oxygen in the bivalent -O-O- structure.

notes.front: Without adequate human data, a liquid or solid is presumed toxic (Division 6.1) if its LD50 for acute oral toxicity is not more than {{c1::300 mg/kg}}.
notes.explanation: Oral, dermal and inhalation results are separate routes; meeting any one is enough.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.132(a)(1)(i), p. 115
notes.evidence: Oral Toxicity. A liquid or solid with an LD50 for acute oral toxicity of not more than 300 mg/kg.

notes.front: Without adequate human data, a material is presumed toxic (Division 6.1) if its LD50 for acute dermal toxicity is not more than {{c1::1000 mg/kg}}.
notes.explanation: The dermal test uses 24 hours of continuous contact with the skin of an albino rabbit.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.132(a)(1)(ii), p. 115
notes.evidence: Dermal Toxicity. A material with an LD50 for acute dermal toxicity of not more than 1000 mg/kg.

notes.front: A dust or mist is presumed toxic (Division 6.1) if its LC50 for acute toxicity on inhalation is not more than {{c1::4 mg/L}}.
notes.explanation: Vapours use a different test: an LC50 of not more than 5000 mL/m3, with a saturated vapour concentration at 20 °C of at least one-fifth of that LC50.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.132(a)(1)(iii)(A), p. 115
notes.evidence: A dust or mist with an LC50 for acute toxicity on inhalation of not more than 4 mg/L; or
uses: LC50 for acute toxicity on inhalation

notes.front: Besides toxicity figures, what other kind of material falls within Division 6.1?
notes.explanation: The definition lists it as a separate route into Division 6.1.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.132(a)(2), p. 115
notes.evidence: Is an irritating material, with properties similar to tear gas, which causes extreme irritation, especially in confined spaces.
notes.back: An irritating material, with properties similar to tear gas, that causes extreme irritation, especially in confined spaces.

notes.front: No human data exist for a liquid pesticide. Its LD50 for acute oral toxicity in rats is 150 mg/kg. It is not corrosive or flammable. Which division fits?
notes.explanation: An oral LD50 of not more than 300 mg/kg makes a liquid or solid presumed toxic.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.132(a)(1)(i), p. 115
notes.evidence: A liquid or solid with an LD50 for acute oral toxicity of not more than 300 mg/kg.
notes.back: B: Division 6.1
notes.choices:
A) Division 2.3
B) Division 6.1
C) Division 6.2
D) Class 9
notes.choicesExplained: A: is for gases, and this material is a liquid. C: is for materials that contain a pathogen. D: is only for materials that meet no other hazard class.

notes.front: A solid's oral LD50 is 2,000 mg/kg, but its dermal LD50 is 600 mg/kg. There are no human data. Does it meet the Division 6.1 definition?
notes.explanation: A dermal LD50 of not more than 1000 mg/kg meets the Division 6.1 presumption on its own.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.132(a)(1)(ii), p. 115
notes.evidence: falls within any one of the following categories when tested on laboratory animals
notes.back: C: Yes, on dermal toxicity
notes.choices:
A) No, because only liquids are tested for dermal toxicity
B) No, because its oral LD50 is above 300 mg/kg
C) Yes, on dermal toxicity
D) Only if it is also a gas
notes.choicesExplained: B: the routes are alternatives; falling within any one category is enough. A: the dermal criterion applies to “a material”, not only to liquids. D: Division 6.1 is for materials other than gases.

notes.front: For Category A, when does an “exposure” occur?
notes.explanation: The Category A definition uses the word “exposure”, and this sentence defines it.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.134(a)(1)(i), p. 120
notes.evidence: An exposure occurs when an infectious substance is released outside of its protective packaging, resulting in physical contact with humans or animals.
notes.back: When the infectious substance is released outside its protective packaging and comes into physical contact with humans or animals.

notes.front: On what may assignment of a substance to Category A be based?
notes.explanation: The regulation lists these as the grounds for the Category A assignment.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.134(a)(1)(i), p. 121
notes.evidence: history or symptoms of the source patient or animal, endemic local conditions, or professional judgment concerning the individual circumstances of the source human or animal.
notes.back: Known medical history or symptoms of the source, endemic local conditions, or professional judgement about the source's circumstances.

notes.front: Are infectious substances sent for diagnostic or investigational purposes included in Category B?
notes.explanation: The Category B definition says so expressly.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.134(a)(1)(ii), p. 121
notes.evidence: This includes Category B infectious substances transported for diagnostic or investigational purposes.
notes.back: Yes, when they are Category B substances.

notes.front: How must a Category B infectious substance be described?
notes.explanation: The regulation fixes this description for every Category B substance.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.134(a)(1)(ii), p. 121
notes.evidence: A Category B infectious substance must be described as ‘‘Biological substance, Category B’’
notes.back: As “Biological substance, Category B”.

notes.front: Category A or Category B: what single question decides it?
notes.explanation: A yes makes it Category A; a substance not generally capable of that is Category B.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.134(a)(1)(ii), p. 121
notes.evidence: An infectious substance that is not in a form generally capable of causing permanent disability or life-threatening or fatal disease in otherwise healthy humans or animals when exposure to it occurs.
notes.back: Is it in a form capable of causing permanent disability or life-threatening or fatal disease in healthy humans or animals on exposure?

notes.front: A clinic ships a patient specimen for diagnosis. The pathogen it may hold is not in a form generally capable of causing permanent disability or fatal disease on exposure. Which category applies?
notes.explanation: Category B covers substances not generally capable of that harm, including those sent for diagnostic purposes.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.134(a)(1)(ii), p. 121
notes.evidence: This includes Category B infectious substances transported for diagnostic or investigational purposes.
notes.back: Category B.

notes.front: A laboratory ships a culture of a pathogen that could cause fatal disease in healthy people if it escaped its packaging and touched them. Which category applies?
notes.explanation: Capacity to cause life-threatening or fatal disease in otherwise healthy humans on exposure is the Category A test.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.134(a)(1)(i), p. 120
notes.evidence: Category A: An infectious substance in a form capable of causing permanent disability or life-threatening or fatal disease in otherwise healthy humans or animals when exposure to it occurs.
notes.back: Category A.

notes.front: Besides skin damage, what else makes a material corrosive (Class 8)?
notes.explanation: The criteria for the corrosion rate are set in § 173.137(c)(2).
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.136(a), p. 124
notes.evidence: A liquid, or a solid which may become liquid during transportation, that has a severe corrosion rate on steel or aluminum based on the criteria in § 173.137(c)(2) is also a corrosive material.
notes.back: A liquid, or a solid that may become liquid in transport, with a severe corrosion rate on steel or aluminium.

notes.front: A liquid cleaner meets no toxicity, flammability or oxidizer criteria. In testing it causes irreversible damage to skin at the point of contact. Which class fits?
notes.explanation: Irreversible skin damage at the site of contact is the Class 8 definition.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.136(a), p. 124
notes.evidence: means a liquid or solid that causes irreversible damage to human skin at the site of contact within a specified period of time.
notes.back: D: Class 8
notes.choices:
A) Division 6.1
B) Class 9
C) Division 5.1
D) Class 8
notes.choicesExplained: A: needs a toxicity criterion such as an oral LD50 of not more than 300 mg/kg. B: is only for materials that meet no other hazard class. C: needs the material to cause or enhance the combustion of other materials.

notes.front: Which Class 9 materials are defined by their effect on a flight crew?
notes.explanation: This is the first group the Class 9 definition names.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.140(a), p. 127
notes.evidence: Any material which has an anesthetic, noxious or other similar property which could cause extreme annoyance or discomfort to a flight crew member so as to prevent the correct performance of assigned duties
notes.back: Materials with an anaesthetic, noxious or similar property that could annoy or discomfort a flight crew member so as to prevent correct performance of duties.

notes.front: What are two materials that fall into Class 9 because they meet a § 171.8 definition?
notes.explanation: Class 9 names these defined groups in paragraph (b).
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.140(b), p. 127
notes.evidence: Any material that meets the definition in § 171.8 of this subchapter for an elevated temperature material, a
notes.back: Any two of: an elevated temperature material; a hazardous substance; a hazardous waste; a marine pollutant.

notes.front: A material meets none of the definitions of Classes 1 to 8, but it has a noxious property that could stop an aircraft's crew from doing their duties. Which class fits?
notes.explanation: Class 9 takes materials that present a transport hazard but meet no other class, including this flight-crew case.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.140(a), p. 127
notes.evidence: which could cause extreme annoyance or discomfort to a flight crew member so as to prevent the correct performance of assigned duties
notes.back: D: Class 9
notes.choices:
A) Division 6.1
B) It is not a hazardous material
C) Class 8
D) Class 9
notes.choicesExplained: A: needs a toxicity criterion or tear-gas-like irritation, not described here. C: needs irreversible skin damage or severe corrosion of steel or aluminium. B: a noxious property affecting a flight crew is named in the Class 9 definition.

notes.front: A consignment holds radionuclides. Its activity concentration exceeds the § 173.436 value, but its total activity does not. Is it radioactive material (Class 7)?
notes.explanation: The definition joins the two tests with “both … and”.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.403, p. 307
notes.evidence: where both the activity concentration and the total activity in the consignment exceed the values specified in the table in § 173.436
notes.back: B: No: both values must be exceeded
notes.choices:
A) Yes: exceeding either value is enough
B) No: both values must be exceeded
C) Yes: any material containing radionuclides is Class 7
D) Yes, because Class 7 heads the order of hazard
notes.choicesExplained: A: the definition needs both the activity concentration and the total activity to exceed the values. C: containing radionuclides is not enough; both activity values must also be exceeded. D: the order ranks classes for materials with several hazards; it does not decide whether a material is Class 7.

notes.front: What does “Forbidden” in column 3 of the § 172.101 table mean for a material?
notes.explanation: Forbidden materials appear in the table in place of a hazard class.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 172.101(d)(1), p. 6
notes.evidence: A material for which the entry in this column is ‘‘Forbidden’’ may not be offered for transportation or transported.
notes.back: It may not be offered for transportation or transported.

notes.front: When does the “Forbidden” prohibition not apply?
notes.explanation: Changing the material's form can take it out of the forbidden entry, but it must then be classed.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 172.101(d)(1), p. 6
notes.evidence: This prohibition does not apply if the material is diluted, stabilized or incorporated in a device and it is classed in accordance with the definitions of hazardous materials contained in part 173 of this subchapter.
notes.back: When the material is diluted, stabilized or incorporated in a device and is classed under the part 173 definitions.

notes.front: What are two things § 173.21 forbids from being offered or transported, unless the regulations provide otherwise?
notes.explanation: Section 173.21 lists further forbidden materials and packages after these two.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.21(a)–(b), p. 31
notes.evidence: the offering for transportation or transportation of the following is forbidden: (a) Materials that are designated ‘‘Forbidden’’ in Column 3 of the § 172.101 table. (b) Forbidden explosives as defined in § 173.54 of this part.
notes.back: Materials marked “Forbidden” in column 3 of the § 172.101 table; forbidden explosives as defined in § 173.54.

notes.front: A chemical's entry in column 3 of the § 172.101 table reads “Forbidden”. A shipper stabilizes it and it is then classed as Division 4.1 under part 173. What follows?
notes.explanation: Dilution, stabilization or incorporation in a device, followed by classing, is the stated exception.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 172.101(d)(1), p. 6
notes.evidence: This prohibition does not apply if the material is diluted, stabilized or incorporated in a device and it is classed in accordance with the definitions of hazardous materials contained in part 173 of this subchapter.
notes.back: A: The prohibition no longer applies to the stabilized, classed material
notes.choices:
A) The prohibition no longer applies to the stabilized, classed material
B) It still may not be offered or transported
C) It may go only with a special permit
D) It becomes Class 9 automatically
notes.choicesExplained: B: the prohibition does not apply once the material is stabilized and classed under part 173. C: the regulation lifts the prohibition on stabilizing and classing, without naming a special permit. D: it is classed by the part 173 definitions, here as Division 4.1.

notes.front: When does the order of hazard in § 173.2a(a) decide a material's class?
notes.explanation: A material listed by name takes the class the table gives it; the order is for the rest.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.2a(a), p. 6
notes.evidence: a material not specifically listed in the § 172.101 Table or assigned to an entry of articles containing hazardous materials (UN3537 to UN3548) that meets the definition of more than one hazard class or division as defined in this part, shall be classed according to the highest applicable hazard class
notes.back: When a material not in the § 172.101 table or its entries for articles containing hazmat meets two or more class definitions.

notes.front: Which class comes first (highest) in the § 173.2a order of hazard?
notes.explanation: Class 7 heads the list; the entry leaves out limited quantities but adds uranium hexafluoride shipped as radioactive material in excepted packages.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.2a(a)(1), p. 6
notes.evidence: (1) Class 7 (radioactive materials, other than limited quantities; and shipments of UN 3507,
notes.back: Class 7, radioactive material (other than limited quantities).

notes.front: After Class 7, the § 173.2a order ranks the gases as Division 2.3, then Division {{c1::2.1}}, then Division 2.2.
notes.explanation: Poisonous gases outrank flammable gases, which outrank non-flammable gases.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.2a(a)(2)–(4), p. 6
notes.evidence: (2) Division 2.3 (poisonous gases). (3) Division 2.1 (flammable gases). (4) Division 2.2 (nonflammable gases).

notes.front: What comes fifth in the § 173.2a order, straight after the gases?
notes.explanation: Only the inhalation hazard liquids in the top danger group rank this high; other Division 6.1 materials come later.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.2a(a)(5), p. 6
notes.evidence: (5) Division 6.1 (poisonous liquids), Packing Group I, poisonous-by-inhalation only.
notes.back: Division 6.1 liquids that are poisonous by inhalation, in the most dangerous group only.

notes.front: Which two Class 4 materials rank sixth and seventh in the § 173.2a order?
notes.explanation: These two outrank the other Class 4 materials, which are ranked by the precedence table.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.2a(a)(6)–(7), p. 6
notes.evidence: A material that meets the definition of a self-reactive material in § 173.124(a)(2) of this subchapter (Division 4.1).
notes.back: Sixth: pyrophoric materials (Division 4.2); seventh: self-reactive materials (Division 4.1).

notes.front: Which two come last in the § 173.2a order of hazard?
notes.explanation: Both come below every class ranked by the precedence table.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.2a(a)(9)–(10), p. 6
notes.evidence: (9) Combustible liquids. (10) Class 9 (miscellaneous hazardous materials).
notes.back: Ninth, combustible liquids; tenth (last), Class 9.

notes.front: A material meets two of Class 3, Class 8 and Divisions 4.1, 4.2, 4.3, 5.1 and 6.1 (outside the higher-ranked cases). What decides its class?
notes.explanation: The table ranks these classes against each other, pair by pair.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.2a(a)(8), p. 6
notes.evidence: The hazard class and packing group for a material meeting more than one of these hazards shall be determined using the precedence table in paragraph (b) of this section.
notes.back: The precedence of hazard table in § 173.2a(b).

notes.front: A Class 1 material also meets another hazard class. How is it classed?
notes.explanation: Class 1 is one of the listed materials the § 173.2a order does not apply to.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.2a(c)(1), p. 7
notes.evidence: A Class 1 (explosive) material that meets any other hazard class or division as defined in this part shall be assigned a division in Class 1.
notes.back: It is assigned a division in Class 1.

notes.front: A Division 5.2 material also meets another hazard class. How is it classed?
notes.explanation: Organic peroxides are one of the listed materials the § 173.2a order does not apply to.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.2a(c)(2), p. 7
notes.evidence: A Division 5.2 (organic peroxide) material that meets the definition of any other hazard class or division as defined in this part, shall be classed as Division 5.2;
notes.back: As Division 5.2.

notes.front: A Division 6.2 material also meets another hazard class other than Class 7. How is it classed?
notes.explanation: Infectious substances are one of the listed materials the § 173.2a order does not apply to.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.2a(c)(3), p. 7
notes.evidence: A Division 6.2 (infectious substance) material that also meets the definition of another hazard class or division, other than Class 7, or that also is a limited quantity Class 7 material, shall be classed as Division 6.2;
notes.back: As Division 6.2 (also when the other hazard is a limited quantity of Class 7).

notes.front: A gas not listed by name in the § 172.101 table meets both the Division 2.1 and the Division 2.3 definitions. How is it classed?
notes.explanation: The order ranks Division 2.3 above Division 2.1.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.2a(a)(2)–(3), p. 6
notes.evidence: (2) Division 2.3 (poisonous gases). (3) Division 2.1 (flammable gases).
notes.back: B: Division 2.3
notes.choices:
A) Division 2.1
B) Division 2.3
C) Both divisions equally
D) Division 2.2
notes.choicesExplained: A: flammable gases rank below poisonous gases in the § 173.2a order. D: non-flammable gases rank below both, and this gas is flammable and poisonous. C: a material is assigned to only one hazard class.

notes.front: A liquid not listed by name meets the Class 3 definition and is also pyrophoric. How is it classed?
notes.explanation: Pyrophoric materials rank sixth in the order, above the classes decided by the precedence table.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.2a(a)(6), p. 6
notes.evidence: (6) A material that meets the definition of a pyrophoric material in
notes.back: A: Division 4.2
notes.choices:
A) Division 4.2
B) Class 3
C) It depends on the precedence table
D) Class 9
notes.choicesExplained: B: Class 3 is ranked in item 8, below pyrophoric materials in item 6. C: the table ranks only materials in item 8; a pyrophoric material ranks above them. D: Class 9 comes last in the order.

notes.front: A diagnostic specimen holds a Category B pathogen in a preservative that meets the Class 3 definition. How is it classed?
notes.explanation: Section 173.2a(c)(3) keeps infectious substances in Division 6.2.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.2a(c)(3), p. 7
notes.evidence: A Division 6.2 (infectious substance) material that also meets the definition of another hazard class or division, other than Class 7,
notes.back: A: Division 6.2
notes.choices:
A) Division 6.2
B) Class 3
C) By the precedence table
D) Class 9
notes.choicesExplained: B: a Division 6.2 material that meets another class (other than Class 7) is classed as Division 6.2. C: Division 6.2 is excluded from the § 173.2a order altogether. D: Class 9 is only for materials that meet no other class.

notes.front: An explosive not otherwise excepted also meets the Class 8 definition. How is it classed?
notes.explanation: Section 173.2a(c)(1) keeps an explosive that meets another class in Class 1.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.2a(c)(1), p. 7
notes.evidence: A Class 1 (explosive) material that meets any other hazard class or division as defined in this part shall be assigned a division in Class 1.
notes.back: B: It is assigned a division in Class 1
notes.choices:
A) Class 8, because corrosion ranks higher
B) It is assigned a division in Class 1
C) By the precedence table
D) Division 6.1
notes.choicesExplained: A: Class 1 materials are taken out of the § 173.2a order and stay in Class 1. C: the table covers Classes 3 and 8 and Divisions 4.1, 4.2, 4.3, 5.1 and 6.1, not Class 1. D: nothing in the case makes the material toxic.

notes.front: A liquid not listed by name is a combustible liquid and also meets the Class 9 definition as a hazardous substance. Which does the order put first?
notes.explanation: Combustible liquids are ninth in the order and Class 9 is tenth.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.2a(a)(9)–(10), p. 6
notes.evidence: (9) Combustible liquids. (10) Class 9 (miscellaneous hazardous materials).
notes.back: D: Combustible liquid
notes.choices:
A) Class 9
B) Class 3
C) Neither; it is not a hazardous material
D) Combustible liquid
notes.choicesExplained: A: Class 9 is tenth, the last item in the order. B: a combustible liquid is not Class 3. C: it meets two definitions, so the order decides between them.
